findings.description:
Context: `AsyncFiller` indexes orders by a truncated, clamped WAD price key. The outer radix trees select the highest bid bucket and lowest ask bucket; orders inside each bucket are ranked by `priorityKey = (priorityFee << 64) | (type(uint64).max - sequence)`, favoring the highest remaining priority fee and then the earliest sequence. Intended price priority requires these tie-breakers to apply only to genuinely equal prices. `AsyncMatching._bookPair` selects orders for both automatic matching through `AsyncSwap.matchNewOrder` and permissionless continuation through `matchBook`. `_matchPair` settles at the older selected order's exact limit, determined by `createdSequence`. Book matches charge no private-fill fee and distribute proceeds and refunds as PoolManager claims. `bestOrder` uses the same bucket-head selection.

```solidity
bidId = book.bestAtPrice(true, bidPrice);
askId = book.bestAtPrice(false, askPrice);
if (_crosses(bidPrice, askPrice, self.orders[bidId], self.orders[askId])) return (bidId, askId);
```

Root cause: `_priceKey` computes `floor(raw quote/asset ratio * PRICE_SCALE)` with `PRICE_SCALE = 1e18`, maps zero to `1`, and saturates values above `type(uint128).max`. Unequal exact limits therefore share a price level. The fixed scale does not account for token decimals or price magnitude: for an 18-decimal asset quoted in six-decimal USDC, the key is approximately `floor(priceUSD * 1e6)`. One key interval represents about 0.1% at $0.001, but about 10% at $0.00001. Prices truncating to zero share key `1` with prices truncating to one; the upper saturation boundary also merges distinct limits.

Within these buckets, `bestAtPrice` ignores exact price and selects only by fee and sequence. `_bookPair` immediately returns those heads when `_crosses` succeeds. That check establishes compatibility, not whether the selected ask is the cheapest or the selected bid is the highest-priced available order. If the heads do not cross, the `exactBounds`/`EligiblePrice` fallback finds priority-ranked crossing alternatives rather than ranking all eligible orders by exact price. It avoids a noncrossing-head obstruction but does not restore best-price execution.

A worse-priced maker can consequently preempt better liquidity either by paying a slightly higher `priorityFee` or, at equal fees, by having an earlier `sequence`. This applies symmetrically to competing asks and bids. The representation is used at creation, by `updatePrice`, and during partial-fill reindexing in `_reduceAfterMatch`, which has its own `_priceKey` implementation. An attacker can therefore enter the shared bucket by creating an order or repricing an existing one. Repricing resets queue sequence but does not defeat a higher-fee advantage, and it preserves `createdSequence`, which determines settlement age.

The affected execution routes include `Router.swap` or another authorized executor's swap/admission path followed by `matchNewOrder`, and continuation through `Router.matchBook`/`AsyncSwap.matchBook`. The same ordering also makes `bestOrder` report a worse exact limit as best.

Severity note: outside the clamped key boundaries, the exact-price gap inside one bucket is less than one raw key interval, so the loss is material only when that interval is large relative to price or the filled quantity is large. Inventory-neutral capture of the spread requires the displaced better order to remain open until a later repurchase; competing fills, cancellations, or repricing can remove that leg. The worse fill itself does not depend on the repurchase.
findings.evidence: Unchanged in current code: AsyncMatching._bookPair (src/libraries/AsyncMatching.sol:176-199) still returns `bestAtPrice` heads (priorityKey = fee<<64 | ~sequence, AsyncFiller.sol:406) as soon as `_crosses` succeeds (line 186); the EligiblePrice fallback is only used when heads don't cross. `_priceKey` still floors to PRICE_SCALE=1e18, clamps 0→1 and saturates at uint128 max (AsyncFiller.sol:446, AsyncMatching.sol:426).
findings.impact: Takers lose available price improvement, better-priced makers are skipped and may never fill, and an attacker can capture the difference by selling ahead of cheaper liquidity and subsequently repurchasing it. Examples: (1) Ordinary bucket: asks selling 1e27 asset units for 10,100 USDC and 10,800 USDC both map to key 10; the worse ask wins by earlier submission at equal fees or by a 110_000 vs 100_000 priority fee; a later 10,800-USDC buyer executes against the worse ask, and the attacker repurchases the honest ask for a ~700 USDC spread (699.79 after priority payments, before gas). (2) Clamped key 1: asks at 100 and 1,000 USDC for the same quantity share key 1; with fees 100_000/110_000 a later bid pays the attacker 1,000 USDC, capturing ~900 USDC (899.79 after fees). (3) Bid side: in an 18-dec PEPE / 6-dec USDC pool, bid A (100 USDC for ~9,174,311 PEPE, 0.10 fee) and bid B (100 USDC for 10,000,000 PEPE, 0.20 fee) share key 10; a seller fills B first, losing ~826,000 PEPE (~8%) of price improvement. (4) Dust closure: asks at 1,100 and 1,800 USDC (fees 100_000/100_001) share key 1; a 1,900-USDC buyer with minOrder 1,000 USDC executes against the worse ask and gets 100 USDC refunded as dust instead of 800 USDC, paying 700 USDC more. Individual exact limits remain respected; no escrow shortfall, insolvency or minimum-output bypass.
findings.recommendation: The report gives no explicit recommendation; implied: rank orders within a shared price bucket by exact price (e.g. via the EligiblePrice exact bounds) before fee/time priority, or use a key with enough resolution that distinct exact limits do not share a level.
findings.title: Coarse `_priceKey` buckets let fee and time priority override better exact limit prices

findings.evidence: AsyncFiller.updatePrice (src/libraries/AsyncFiller.sol:255-276) still only checks owner, newAmountOutMin != 0, liveness and checkMinimum, then rewrites amountOutMin/price/sequence; there is no check of info.priorityFee against minPriorityFee(newAmountOutMin) and no top-up.
findings.impact: Qualifying sell orders can subsequently be matched, filled—including against LP liquidity when their terms are met—or cancelled while paying less than the mandatory priority bid for their final terms. FeeVault loses up to 100,000 USDC base units ($0.10) per order; the 10-to-1,000-USDC example avoids $0.09. Repetition reduces protocol revenue and weakens the mandatory bid's anti-spam and cancellation deterrent. Depends on pool minimums permitting an initial bid below the final requirement; makers still fund input and gas. It grants no higher queue priority, does not touch other makers' escrow or bypass the filler output fee.
findings.recommendation: The report gives no explicit recommendation; implied: in `AsyncFiller.updatePrice`, require (or top up) `priorityFee >= minPriorityFee(newAmountOutMin)` for sell orders.
findings.title: `updatePrice` lets sell orders retain a priority bid below the minimum required for their new terms

findings.evidence: Router.cancelWithSig (src/Router.sol:200-211) is still the only writer of cancelNonceUsed (footprint: writes [cancelNonceUsed]); no other Router function writes it, and Router does not read AsyncSwap.nonceUsed. The digest still binds orderId, amountIn, nonce, deadline only.
findings.impact: A maker who handed a signed cancel to a relayer cannot take it back. The relayer, or anyone who saw the signature, can cancel the order at any point up to `deadline` while the stored `amountIn` equals the signed amount, even after the maker calls `AsyncSwap.invalidateNonce`. The same applies if an identical order id recurs with the same `amountIn` before the deadline (closed by another path and re-placed in the same block). The maker loses the order's book position and time priority and the remaining escrowed `priorityFee`, forfeited to FeeVault; the input amount is refunded, so principal is not stolen.
findings.recommendation: The report gives no explicit recommendation; implied: add a Router function letting makers invalidate cancel nonces (or have the Router consult the hook's nonceUsed / AsyncSwap.invalidateNonce), and/or bind signed cancels to a per-order state that changes when the order closes.
findings.title: Signed cancellations cannot be revoked and stay valid after the order is closed by other means

summary: Automated auditor scan of AsyncSwap, a Uniswap v4 hook that turns exact-input swaps into escrowed limit orders settled by book matching, pool liquidity or external fillers. It reports one medium issue (coarse price buckets letting fee/time priority override better exact prices) and two low issues (updatePrice not topping up the priority bid, and irrevocable signed cancellations).
